author: ohtadmin
title: Proposals sought to turn Knowles site into housing
text:
A request for proposals seeking developers to transform the former ambulance barn into affordable housing will need amendments before the town council votes to advertise it.
The draft was presented to the councilors Monday at their meeting. Councilwoman Mary Meagher and Town Administrator Ed Mello were the only ones to offer input.
“This is great,” she said. “I’m so happy to see something put into print.”
“I emphasize draft,” Mello said. “We need some direction.”
The municipally owned property at 11 Knowles Court is 13,678 square feet with a 2,500-square-foot concrete block garage. An “unconfirmed review” indicates the property could accommodate a combination of nine one- and two-bedroom units.
The request for proposals seeks the “development of a maximum number of residential year-round rentals” with two-thirds of the units at 80 percent of the area median income or less. The remaining units would be up to 100 percent of the area median income.
It said “a high percentage of the dwelling units on site shall be for families of more than one individual and a minimum of two bedrooms.” The development must be “consistent and compatible with surrounding existing development.”
Meagher, despite her optimism, recommended changes. The “major piece” she called problematic was asking bidders “for too much.” When the RFP initially was advertised for the Looking Upwards project at Hammett Court, the document requested for bidders to “do all these drawings.”
“It seemed like such a great idea,” she said. “We got absolutely zero responses.”
Meagher, in hindsight, said bidders are not “going to give you all that work for free” if they are not guaranteed to have a job. She suggested fewer demands.
Mello mentioned two obstacles that have stalled other cities and towns from attracting bidders. First, municipalities that didn’t commit to their advertised properties being earmarked for affordable housing were unsuccessful. There were concerns with seeking proposals before “fully vetting” the potential development.
“Some communities were floating the idea and hoping to get a response,” he said.
Second, Mello said 11 Knowles Court is zoned as public property. There could be “hesitation from potential developers” if the property is not zoned residential.
The affordable housing committee will consider amendments to the request for proposals before it again goes before the councilors, Mello said.
